steps.text:
On day one, we recommend starting with ball mastery.

• It's one of the most important skills you can learn.

• You don't need any equipment.

• You can do it in your living room, your garage, or out on the field.

Here are a few ball mastery programs to get you started.
steps.label: Day One: Start with Ball Mastery

player.q: Do you recommend a training plan?

steps.label: Yes — But It Depends on Your Preference
steps.text:
Training plans are recurring and give you a guided path.

• However, some users prefer sticking with a few favorite folders and working through them at their own pace.

• I use both.

• I built a custom plan for my son's after-school training, and I favorite folders and videos for when we train outside together.

player.q: How long should my child train?

steps.label: The Key to Success: Train at a Level They Can Stick With
steps.text:
We call this **MEEE** — the Minimum Extra Effort they can do with Enthusiasm.

A few things to keep in mind:

• Consistency beats intensity — even **20 minutes a week** can meaningfully improve a player's skill

• Sit down with your child and set a weekly goal together, one they can realistically handle

• Let them help pick the goal — a goal they chose is a goal they'll keep

coach.intro: Your first three weeks as a coach. Do them in order — each one sets up the next.

steps.label: Day 1
steps.text: Set up the team and set your goals: team name, logo, and the weekly training goal you want players held to.

steps.label: Week 1
steps.text: Get your players on. Onboard the ones waiting to join, then check the roster so you know who is actually active.

steps.label: Week 1
steps.text: Assign the first homework from the Coach’s Board. Start small — one folder with a due date beats a long list nobody finishes.

steps.label: Week 2
steps.text: Check who trained, then run something competitive. The 24 to 48 Hour Challenge is the easiest one to start with.
